extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 subject matter eligibility, including claim interpretation (BRI), application of the Alice/Mayo two‑part test, Pathways A/B/C, and related procedural practices for examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories requirement (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter (35 U.S.C. 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that the claim as a whole falls within at least one category (process/machine/manufacture/composition). For non-process categories, the subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. If the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) covers material not found in any of the four categories, the claim falls outside §101 and should be rejected. If the BRI covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1. If amendable to fall within a statutory category, recommend narrowing amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions exclusion (Step 2 principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, the claimed invention must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter — the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena/products of nature) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether claim limitations align with at least one judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). If the claim is directed to an exception, analyze whether additional elements provide 'significantly more' (an 'inventive concept') per the Alice/Mayo framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Alice/Mayo two‑part test (use as the sole framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Alice/Mayo two‑part test to evaluate eligibility: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo two‑part test is the only test that should be used. The second part is described as a search for an 'inventive concept.' Conduct Step 2A first; only proceed to Step 2B if Step 2A finds the claim directed to an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI sets claim boundaries and influences whether claim seeks to cover subject matter beyond statutory categories or encompasses exceptions. Claim interpretation can affect both Step 1 and Step 2 determinations. Consider the specification when construing claim terms under BRI. If BRI covers non‑statutory embodiments, point them out and recommend amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways A/B/C eligibility flow (streamlined and full analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three pathways to eligibility: Pathway A (self‑evident eligibility — streamlined), Pathway B (claim falls within statutory category and is not directed to a judicial exception), Pathway C (claim falls within statutory category, is directed to a judicial exception, but recites additional elements amounting to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis (Pathway A) is appropriate, conduct full Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Claims that could be eligible under Pathway A but are subjected to full analysis will still be eligible at Pathway B or C if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non‑statutory product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to any of the statutory categories include: products that do not have a physical or tangible form (e.g., data per se, computer program per se claimed as a product), transitory forms of signal transmission (signals per se), and subject matter statutorily prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product claim to software expressed as code or instructions detached from any medium lacks physical embodiment; such product claims without structural recitations do not fall within statutory categories. Transitory propagating signals lack the concrete structure to be a machine/manufacture/composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of the four statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify what each statutory category means: process = act or series of acts (method); machine = concrete thing consisting of parts/devices; manufacture = tangible article given a new form/quality/property by human action; composition of matter = combination of two or more substances or composite articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining Step 1, verify claim elements satisfy the relevant category definition (e.g., machines/ manufactures/ compositions require physical/tangible form). It is not necessary to pick a single category if the claim clearly falls within at least one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation can change eligibility outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction (in light of the specification and BRI) can be decisive in determining whether a claim is statutory, directed to an exception, or recites significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relevant case law examples: interpretations that broaden claims to include non‑statutory embodiments (e.g., carrier waves) can cause Step 1 failure; constructions that require concrete technical limitations can support finding 'not directed to an abstract idea' or provide 'significantly more.' Consider 35 U.S.C. 112(f) functional claim interpretations where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine‑or‑transformation test as a clue, not a separate test
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine‑or‑transformation test is an important clue to eligibility but should not be used as a separate test; it should be considered in the 'significantly more' analysis (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat evidence that a claim is tied to a particular machine or effects a particular transformation as supportive of eligibility under Step 2B, but do not treat the test as dispositive on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern underlies the eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying concern driving the Alice/Mayo framework is preemption: patents should not monopolize basic tools (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) such that innovation is impeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While preemption is not a standalone test, consider whether the claim would effectively preempt use of the underlying exception; lack of preemption can support eligibility, while broad preemptive claims weigh against it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to technology or computer functionality (Step 2B factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that improves the functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field can supply 'significantly more' and weigh toward eligibility under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim elements produce a technological improvement (not merely an abstract idea implemented on a computer), identify and reference specification portions describing the improvement. Examples include improvements to existing technology or to computer functionality recognized by case law (e.g., Enfish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine requirement (Step 2B factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting a claim to a particular machine (or an unconventional use of a machine) can support a finding of 'significantly more' under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how the claim's machine limitation is specific and meaningful (not merely a generic computer). Generic computer implementation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation requirement (Step 2B factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim effecting a particular transformation of matter to a different state or thing can qualify as 'significantly more' under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the claimed process effects a concrete transformation (Gottschalk v. Benson, Diehr) rather than merely manipulating or organizing information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on well‑understood, routine, conventional activity to supply 'significantly more' (Step 2B negative factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are well‑understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the industry do not amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional claim elements are generic computer functions or commonplace steps, they are unlikely to transform an exception into patent‑eligible subject matter. Examiners should identify and explain why elements are routine/conventional when making a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations and non‑generic arrangements (Step 2B considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be eligible if they recite other meaningful limitations or a non‑generic arrangement of known, conventional elements that provide unconventional technical solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ordered combinations and non‑generic arrangements that achieve an unconventional technical result; cite specification or claim construction that shows the limitation is more than a mere instruction to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient (Step 2B negative factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere instructions to apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., 'apply the formula') do not supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discern whether the claim simply tells practitioners to implement an exception without adding a technical solution; such claims should be treated as ineligible absent additional meaningful limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra‑solution activity does not confer eligibility (Step 2B negative factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra-solution activities that are insignificant to the claimed invention (administrative or conventional data-gathering, generic post‑solution activity) do not render an ineligible claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether added steps merely nominally tie the exception to a particular environment or add meaningless post‑solution tasks. Such insignificant additions should not be considered 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use or technological environment limitations are generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or technological environment (e.g., 'on the Internet' or 'in banking') does not, by itself, make the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field‑of‑use or environment restrictions should not be credited as providing 'significantly more' unless they contribute a meaningful, technical improvement or unconventional limitation beyond the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self‑evident (2106.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self‑evident (claims clearly fall within a statutory category and are plainly eligible), a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be used to find claims eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use streamlined analysis for clear cases, but if uncertain, perform full Alice/Mayo analysis to promote consistency and correctness. Claims that are arguably eligible under Pathway A but undergo full analysis will be found eligible under Pathway B or C if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use superseded tests (e.g., 'useful, concrete, and tangible result'; 'special purpose computer' alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility should not be evaluated based on the 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test (State Street/Alappat) or on merely adding a generic or 'special purpose' computer to an otherwise ineligible claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that tests such as State Street's 'useful, concrete and tangible result' and the In re Alappat 'special purpose computer' rationale have been superseded by Bilski and Alice; rely instead on Alice/Mayo analysis and related precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other statutory provisions; §101 is a threshold inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold test; even if an invention is eligible under §101, it must still satisfy other Patent Act requirements such as novelty (§102), nonobviousness (§103), and written description/enablement (§112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should conduct complete examinations under §§102, 103, 112 (and utility/other requirements) regardless of §101 determinations. Use statutory provisions to address patentability concerns not resolved by §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and recordkeeping guidance for §101 rejections and allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a §101 rejection, use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05 and 7.05.01) and explain the BRI or deficiencies; when claims are found eligible, clarifying remarks referencing specification and elements producing improvements may be made on the record (including with a Notice of Allowance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear explanations in the record to aid applicant understanding and prosecution. When recommending amendments to avoid non‑statutory embodiments, explain examples and suggest narrowing language. Clarifying remarks are useful both for allowances and for explaining the rationale for rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and labeling of judicial exceptions (no strict bright lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions can be described using varied terms (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas, physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied algorithms). There are no bright lines between exception types; many concepts overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For §101 analysis, it suffices for the examiner to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. Be mindful that certain concepts (e.g., mathematical formulas) can be characterized under multiple exception labels.
